summary: The v12 composite improvement (precomputed maxHiP1, orientation-level skip, 5 orderings, culprit repair) was tested against the v10 baseline across 3 seeds. The hypothesis that v12 would outperform v10 by 2-4 points was refuted: v12 averaged 81.90 vs v10's 82.62 (paired mean difference -0.71, t=-0.787, p>>0.05). The v10 baseline remains the best-performing variant at a stable ~83 score plateau.
key_points: REFUTED: v12 (mean 81.90, std 0.70) did not beat v10 (mean 82.62, std 1.30). Paired differences were +0.12, -2.52, +0.26 — statistically indistinguishable from zero.
Design-phase back-to-back probes (+6.29, +3.84 for v12) were misleading artifacts of system load variance; the formal alternating-execution experiment showed no real effect.
CONFIRMED: v10 control scored 82.62 ± 1.30, consistent with iter-4's 82.71 mean, validating measurement stability.

Root cause analysis: the four v12 enhancements roughly cancel each other — speed savings from maxHiP1 precomputation are tiny (~14ms), extra orderings don't add meaningful diversity, and culprit repair consumes time that random restarts would use more effectively.

The system appears to be at a hardware-limited plateau (~83) for the greedy skyline approach. Further gains likely require a fundamentally different algorithmic strategy (e.g., bottom-left with backtracking, simulated annealing over placements, or NFDH/FFDH strip-packing variants).
